body.head: Theatrical Examiner.
body.p:
The episode of Raymond and Agnes, from Mr. Lewis’s Novel of The Monk, forces itself upon our attention this week, from the circumstance of its having been brought before the town at two of our Theatres, at Covent Garden in the shape of the revived Pantomime of Raymond and Agnes, or the Castle of Lindenburgh, and at the Haymarket in the guise of a new Melo-Drama, called Travellers Benighted, or the Forest of Rosenwald. We are sorry to see that the public taste for Mr. Lewis’s horrors is not yet worn out. At the Haymarket indeed, where the German school has been so lately ridiculed by the performance of the jeu d’esprit from the Anti-Jacobin, it was ludicrously inconsistent in the Manager to sanction the production of Travellers Benighted, and the piece was justly damned on the first night; but damnation seems now-a-days to be of no more injury to a play, than our criticisms. We witnessed the growth of Mr. Lewis’s Wood Daemon into One o'Clock, during the summer, with the greatest disgust; and we are now called upon decidedly to protest against the legitimacy of such dramas. It would be affectation to deny their interest; it is most powerful; it is too powerful; but how is it brought about? by the fair engines of tragedy? by means of terror and pity? No; by means of horror and agony: it is an interest
"By many a foul and midnight murder fed;" it is the interest which makes old women and children creep closer round the fire at a story of ghosts: its terror is that with which the Newgate Calendar is read, and its pity is that of those women who call every man going to be hanged, a handsome, proper youth: in a word, it is the tragic interest over which Mr. Nares, the Magistrate, presides; and if the inhabitants of the Felons’ side were to command a play, they ought to crown Mr. M. G. Lewis their Poet-laureat. To enter into a criticism of the Novel of the Monk, would lead us beyond the limits of our Paper: whatever may be the opinion as to its morality, it is a decided proof of the author's genius for powerful writing, although he cannot be called original, either in his super-human or his human incidents. The former may all be traced to old ballads, zests, romances, contes, and fabliaux; and as to the latter, the adventure in the forest before us was in a great measure anticipated by Count Fathom's betrayment into the wood, and escape by means of the old woman; and indeed, Fathom’s meeting with the supposed Ghost of Monimia in the church, may have furnished Mr. Lewis with another hint for his novel. While we are upon this subject, we cannot help remarking upon the beauty and vigour of style in which Smollett has told all these interesting adventures, and how much greater a master of language he has shewn himself than Fielding. Smollett often rises to the dignity of epic story, even in his novels; but Fielding was quite incapable of quitting the path of comic epopee, and could no more have written a history than a tragedy.

The dramatic pieces before us are precisely the same, scene for scene, excepting that that at Covent Garden is pantomime, and that at the Haymarket is provided with words. And such words! the actors might each have furnished their own, as they went along, as they in fact did, for aught we know, and they would have been as good. Mr. Lewis himself cannot have written Travellers Benighted; he is no very competent penner of dialogue; but he could not have done so bad as this. The denouements of both pieces are made to differ from the novel, inasmuch as, though Don Raymond does abscond with the real ghost instead of the sham, she leads him only to the next scene, like Hamlet’s Ghost, and there descends a trap, whence rises a cloud, inscribed, in red capitals, "Protect the Child of murder'd Agnes." The said masquerading child again falls into the Banditti's hands, and is by them carried into a cave, from which she is rescued again by Raymond, who leads her to the altar, where the Ghost again appears to remove her father's scruples against her marriage.

We are happy to think that the run of these pieces will not be very long. The performance at Covent Garden, which we witnessed on Friday evening, was very thinly attended, and very equivocally received; and yet the splendour with which the piece is gotten up at this house would insure success to a less horrible and disgusting spectacle. Mr. Grimaldi performs the part of the first murderer at this house; and at the Haymarket the part is allotted to Mr. Elliston. Both actors are out of their line: we were now and then tempted to laugh at the former, and we pitied the latter, who occasionally, however, threw in a few tones which were natural and beautiful. We need dwell no longer upon these gaol-bird horrors and Bartholomew-fair apparitions: they have had their day, and their downfall is fast approaching.

A young lady, who is by one of the daily papers called Miss Waring, and by another Mrs. Chill, made her first appearance on Friday night, as a substitute for Mrs. Dickons, in the bad opera of the Woodman. Her person, if not beautiful, is pleasing; and her figure very strongly reminded us of Mrs. Mathews, than whom she is a little taller. Like most singers, she seems to have paid little attention to the art of acting, and to have devoted herself entirely to the science of music. For this, she has certainly very many and charming requisites: her voice is not so powerful as that of her predecessor, Mrs. Dickons; but her execution is quite as correct, as far as we have heard it. Her tones are delicate and harmonic, like the vibrations of musical glasses; and her taste seems very considerable. Her reception was truly flattering; and we are of opinion, that Mrs. Chill, alias Miss Waring, will prove no inconsiderable addition to our English musical talent.

Mr. Incledon, as well as Mrs. Dickons, is on the list of absentees from Covent-Garden this season. How true is Dr. Johnson's observation, that in this world nobody is missed! His place has been even better supplied than that of Mrs. Dickons, by Mr. Sinclair, who performed Wilford in the Opera of Friday. He too is no actor: his person is tall and thin, and we agree with him in wishing he could get rid of his arms. His voice is most delightful, and his falsetto quite unique; he will doubtless ripen into a most accomplished singer. His grace-notes are evidently studied upon those of Mr. Braham; but he has more voice than that masterly singer, if he do not turn it to such great account. Mr. Sinclair's shake is quite perfect, whereas Mr. Braham's is a notorious trick. We should be glad to hear both our vocal debutants in a duet: why is there not such a thing in the Woodman? Their voices seem peculiarly adapted to each other, from their mutual delicacy and unobtrusiveness. Hence the beautiful glees with which Mr. Shield has enriched the Opera, went off with the completest effect on Friday night. It must be a great gratification to a composer to write for such singers as Mr. Sinclair and the Lady; for they have no bad tricks to flatter, and, as far as we know, no glaring deficiencies to hide. We should be glad to see Mr. Shield once more employed in so agreeable a task.
